subject: biology
title: C3.1 Integration of body systems
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: C3.1 Integration of body systems — IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025), topic C3.1.
meta_desc: IB DP Biology practice covering C3.1 Integration of body systems, guide topic C3.1.
final_note: You worked through C3.1 Integration of body systems — 23 guide statements.

concepts.def: The coordination of the component parts of a living system so that together they perform an overall function that no part could perform alone. Integration is a necessary process in living systems at every level, from organelles within a cell to organs within a body.

The organization of a multicellular organism in levels: cells are grouped into tissues (groups of similar cells performing a shared function), tissues into organs, organs into body systems, and body systems into the whole organism. Each level is a subsystem of the level above and is integrated with the others.

A property of a whole system that its component parts do not have on their own and that arises from the interaction of those parts. A cheetah becoming an effective predator is an emergent property of the integration of its muscular, skeletal, nervous, respiratory and circulatory systems; no single system makes it a predator.

Communication between organs by electrical impulses conducted along neurons, with chemical transmission across synapses. A message travels rapidly along a fixed pathway of neurons to a specific target, so nervous responses are fast, precisely targeted and usually short-lived.

Communication between organs by hormones, chemical messengers secreted by endocrine glands directly into the blood. The blood carries a hormone to every part of the body, but only cells with receptors for that hormone respond. Hormonal responses are typically slower to begin and longer-lasting than nervous responses, and one hormone can affect many organs at once.

The movement of materials between organs by the circulating blood, which integrates organs that are far apart. Examples: oxygen absorbed in the lungs is carried to respiring tissues; glucose absorbed in the small intestine is carried to the liver and to muscles; urea produced by the liver is carried to the kidneys; and hormones are carried from endocrine glands to their target organs.

concepts.term: Brain as central information integration organ
concepts.def: The brain receives information from many receptors at once, combines it with stored information from previous experience and uses the combined result to decide on responses. This processing of combined inputs, together with learning (changes in behaviour as a result of experience) and memory (the storage and later retrieval of information), makes the brain the central integrating organ of the body.

A conscious process is one of which the person is aware and which involves processing in the cerebral hemispheres, such as deciding to pick up a cup. An unconscious process takes place without awareness or a decision, such as a reflex or the adjustment of heart rate; it can be integrated in the spinal cord or in parts of the brain such as the medulla, without the cerebral hemispheres deciding on the response.

concepts.term: Spinal cord as an integrating centre
concepts.def: The part of the central nervous system inside the vertebral column, with grey matter (cell bodies, interneurons and synapses) surrounded by white matter (myelinated nerve fibres). As well as conducting impulses to and from the brain, the spinal cord integrates unconscious processes such as reflexes: it receives sensory input and sends motor output without the cerebral hemispheres being involved in the decision.

A cell that detects a stimulus (a change in the internal or external environment) and produces a signal that is passed to a sensory neuron. Examples are photoreceptor cells in the retina and hair cells in the cochlea. In the skin, the free nerve ending of a sensory neuron itself acts as a pain receptor.

A neuron that conveys messages, as nerve impulses, from receptor cells to the central nervous system. Sensory neurons provide the input to the spinal cord and, via the spinal cord or the cranial nerves, to the cerebral hemispheres. Impulses travel along a sensory neuron in one direction only, towards the CNS.

A neuron that carries nerve impulses from the central nervous system to an effector. Motor neurons carrying output from the cerebral hemispheres end at skeletal muscle fibres, where their impulses stimulate the muscle to contract. A muscle can only be stimulated to contract; it relaxes when stimulation stops and is lengthened by the contraction of an antagonistic muscle.

A bundle of nerve fibres (the long axons of neurons) enclosed in a protective sheath of connective tissue. Most nerves contain fibres of both sensory and motor neurons, so a single nerve carries impulses towards the CNS in some fibres and away from it in others. A neuron is a single cell; a nerve contains fibres from many neurons.

In a transverse section of a nerve, a myelinated fibre appears as an axon surrounded by a thick myelin sheath, formed by Schwann cells wrapped around it, which insulates the axon and greatly increases the speed at which impulses are conducted. An unmyelinated fibre has no such sheath and conducts more slowly. Both types are normally present in the same nerve.

The pathway of neurons that produces a reflex: a rapid, involuntary response to a stimulus that does not require a decision by the brain. In the pain reflex of the hand, a free sensory nerve ending acts as the pain receptor; the sensory neuron carries the impulse to the grey matter of the spinal cord, where a single interneuron passes it to a motor neuron, which stimulates skeletal muscle in the arm (the effector) to contract and withdraw the hand.

A neuron located entirely within the central nervous system that connects other neurons. In the pain reflex arc a single interneuron in the grey matter of the spinal cord links the sensory neuron to the motor neuron. Other interneurons pass the sensory information up the spinal cord to the brain, so the pain is felt shortly after the reflex has already withdrawn the hand.

The structure that carries out the response to a stimulus: a muscle or a gland. In the pain reflex the effector is skeletal muscle, which is stimulated to contract even though the response is involuntary; being skeletal muscle does not make a response voluntary.

A region of the brain, below and behind the cerebral hemispheres, that coordinates the contraction of skeletal muscles and maintains balance and posture. It does not initiate voluntary movements, which are commanded by the cerebral hemispheres; it uses information from the eyes, the inner ear and receptors in muscles and joints to make movements smooth, accurate and well-timed.

A cycle of physiological activity with a period of about 24 hours, generated within the body and synchronized to the day–night cycle by light detected by the eyes. The cycle of sleeping and waking is a circadian rhythm.

A hormone secreted by the pineal gland in the brain in a diurnal pattern: secretion rises in the evening as light fades, is highest during the night and falls to a low level during the day, because light detected by the retina suppresses it. A high melatonin concentration promotes sleepiness, so the pattern helps to establish the cycle of sleeping and waking.

A hormone secreted by the adrenal glands, above the kidneys, in response to danger, stress or the anticipation of vigorous activity. Its widespread effects prepare the body for intense muscle contraction: heart rate and stroke volume increase; bronchioles dilate and ventilation increases; glycogen in the liver is broken down, raising blood glucose; blood is diverted to skeletal muscle by vasodilation there and vasoconstriction in the gut and skin; and the pupils dilate.

A region of the brain that links the nervous system and the endocrine system. It monitors conditions in the blood, such as temperature and solute concentration, receives information from other parts of the brain, and controls the pituitary gland so that the pituitary secretes the hormones the body needs.

A small endocrine gland attached beneath the hypothalamus. Under the control of the hypothalamus it secretes hormones, some of which act directly on body tissues (for example growth hormone and ADH) and some of which control other endocrine glands (for example TSH controls the thyroid gland, and FSH and LH control the gonads). Through the pituitary, the hypothalamus controls much of the endocrine system.

A stretch receptor in the walls of the aorta and the carotid arteries that monitors blood pressure. When blood pressure rises the artery wall is stretched more and the baroreceptors send impulses more frequently to the medulla.

A receptor that monitors the chemical composition of the blood: its pH and its concentrations of oxygen and carbon dioxide. Chemoreceptors are located in the walls of the aorta and the carotid arteries (the aortic and carotid bodies) and in the medulla of the brainstem.

The part of the brainstem that coordinates the unconscious control of heart rate and ventilation. Its cardiovascular centre receives impulses from baroreceptors and chemoreceptors and sends nerve impulses to the heart: impulses along the sympathetic nerve increase heart rate and stroke volume, and impulses along the parasympathetic (vagus) nerve decrease heart rate. Its respiratory centre sends impulses to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles.
The volume of blood pumped out of a ventricle in one heartbeat. Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume, so the medulla can increase the output of the heart by increasing either or both.

Cell respiration produces carbon dioxide, which dissolves in blood plasma and forms carbonic acid; this releases hydrogen ions and lowers blood pH. Chemoreceptors in the brainstem detect the fall in pH and the respiratory centre of the medulla sends more frequent impulses to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles, increasing the rate and depth of ventilation. More carbon dioxide is exhaled, blood pH rises back towards normal and the stimulus is removed: negative feedback.
Waves of contraction of the circular and longitudinal smooth muscle in the wall of the gut that move material along it. Peristalsis is involuntary and does not depend on gravity.

A network of neurons in the wall of the gut that controls peristalsis and other gut activity involuntarily, without instructions from the CNS. The ENS coordinates the contractions of the gut wall so that material passes along the gut in an orderly way at a rate suited to digestion and absorption. Initiation of swallowing and egestion of faeces are under voluntary control by the CNS; peristalsis between these points is controlled by the ENS.

A qualitative observation is a description without numerical measurement, such as a labelled diagram recording that a seedling shoot has curved towards the light. A quantitative observation is a numerical measurement, such as the angle of curvature of the shoot measured with a protractor in degrees. Both are valid scientific data.

Precision is how closely repeated measurements of the same quantity agree with each other; it is limited by the resolution of the instrument (for example a protractor marked in 1° divisions) and by random error. Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true value; it is reduced by systematic error, such as aligning the protractor against the wrong reference line. Reliability is the consistency of results when the investigation is repeated; it is improved by using many seedlings and repeating the experiment. Repeating measurements reduces the effect of random error but does not remove a systematic error.

The directional growth of a plant shoot towards a source of light coming from one side. A tropism is a growth response in which the direction of growth is determined by the direction of the stimulus. Phototropism is caused by cells on the shaded side of the shoot elongating more than cells on the lit side; it is growth, not movement of existing tissues.

A signalling chemical produced by plant cells that regulates growth, development or responses to stimuli in other cells, usually at very low concentrations. Plants use a variety of chemicals as phytohormones, including auxins, cytokinins, gibberellins, abscisic acid and the gas ethylene. Plants have no endocrine glands: phytohormones are produced in many tissues and move from cell to cell or in the xylem and phloem.

A membrane protein that actively transports auxin out of a plant cell. Auxin can diffuse freely into cells but cannot diffuse out, so the position of the efflux carriers determines the direction in which auxin leaves. When all the cells in a tissue concentrate their efflux carriers on the same side, auxin is transported from cell to cell in one direction and becomes concentrated in part of the plant, maintaining a concentration gradient.

The continuous network of cell walls and intercellular spaces outside the plasma membranes of plant cells. Auxin promotes the secretion of hydrogen ions from the cytoplasm into the apoplast, which acidifies the cell wall.

concepts.term: Promotion of cell growth by auxin
concepts.def: Auxin stimulates proton pumps in the plasma membrane to secrete hydrogen ions into the apoplast. The resulting low pH in the cell wall loosens the cross links between cellulose molecules, so the wall can stretch and the cell elongates as it takes up water. In a shoot lit from one side, auxin is concentrated on the shaded side, so cells there elongate more and the difference in growth rate bends the shoot towards the light.

A phytohormone produced in root tips and transported to the shoots, where it promotes shoot growth. Auxin is produced in shoot tips and transported to the roots. The interaction between the two phytohormones ensures that root and shoot growth remain integrated: each organ signals its growth to the other, so neither outgrows what the other can support.

A gaseous phytohormone (IUPAC name: ethene) that stimulates the changes in fruits that occur during ripening, such as softening of cell walls, conversion of starch to sugars and changes in colour. Because it is a gas, ethylene diffuses through the air from one fruit to neighbouring fruits.

A control mechanism in which the response increases the original stimulus, so the process accelerates. Ethylene stimulates ripening, and ripening stimulates the fruit to produce more ethylene, which spreads to neighbouring cells and fruits. As a result the ripening of a fruit, and of the fruits on a plant, is rapid and synchronized, which benefits the plant by making its fruit attractive to seed-dispersing animals at the same time.

mcqs.q: Which statement best describes what is meant by integration in a living system?
options: Coordination of the component parts so that together they perform an overall function that none performs alone.
Each component part performs its own function independently, so the parts do not need to interact.
A single dominant part carries out the overall function while the other parts play no role in it.
Coordination is achieved only by conscious decisions, so it applies only to organisms with a brain.
mcqs.specStatementText: Parts of a living system must work together
mcqs.explain: Integration is a necessary process in living systems: coordination is needed for the component parts of a system to collectively perform an overall function.
rationales: Integration is a necessary process in living systems: coordination is needed for the component parts of a system to collectively perform an overall function.
A student who pictures body systems as separate machines picks this. Parts that do not interact cannot perform a collective function; integration is the coordination between them.
A student who assigns each function to one 'responsible' system picks this. An overall function of a system emerges from all its parts working together, not from one part alone.
A student who equates coordination with conscious control picks this. Integration occurs at every level of living systems, including unconscious processes and organisms with no brain at all.

mcqs.q: A cheetah can sprint at over 100 km per hour and catch fast-moving prey. Why is its effectiveness as a predator described as an emergent property?
options: It is a property of the muscular system alone, because the muscles are what make the cheetah run so fast.
It arises from the integration of several body systems and is not a property of any one of them on its own.
It is a property already present in each of its muscle cells; the whole animal simply has many of them.
Each of its body systems has its own separate ability, and the cheetah's speed is simply the sum of these separate abilities.
mcqs.specStatementText: Cells build tissues, organs and systems, and new properties emerge
mcqs.explain: An emergent property arises from the interaction of the parts of a system. A cheetah becomes an effective predator by integration of its body systems; the property is not possessed by any one of them.
rationales: A student who matches each function to one system picks this. Muscles cannot run without nervous control, a skeleton to act on and oxygen and glucose delivered by the blood; the speed emerges from all of these together.

An emergent property arises from the interaction of the parts of a system. A cheetah becomes an effective predator by integration of its body systems; the property is not possessed by any one of them.

A student who thinks higher levels only scale up the properties of cells picks this. A single muscle cell can contract but cannot hunt; hunting is a new property that emerges at the level of the integrated organism.

A student who sees the systems as working independently picks this. An emergent property is more than the sum of the parts' abilities: it depends on their coordination, which none of them has separately.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the roles of the nervous system and the endocrine system in sending messages between organs?
options: Hormones are carried along nerves to their target organs, while nerve impulses are carried around the body in the blood plasma.
Both systems produce equally rapid responses that last equally long, and differ only in the chemical that carries the message.
Nervous messages travel as impulses along neurons to specific targets; hormones are carried by the blood to every organ.
The blood carries each hormone only to its target organ, in the same way that a nerve reaches only one target.
mcqs.specStatementText: Nerves, hormones and blood link organs together
mcqs.explain: The nervous system sends electrical impulses along fixed pathways of neurons to particular cells. The endocrine system secretes hormones into the blood, which carries them everywhere; only cells with receptors respond.
rationales: A student who has merged the two systems into one set of wires picks this. Hormones travel in the blood and nerve impulses travel along neurons; the routes are not interchangeable.

A student who thinks of an 'adrenaline rush' as instantaneous picks this. Nervous responses take milliseconds; hormonal responses are slower to start and longer-lasting, and the nervous message is electrical, not a chemical carried in blood.

The nervous system sends electrical impulses along fixed pathways of neurons to particular cells. The endocrine system secretes hormones into the blood, which carries them everywhere; only cells with receptors respond.
A student who reads 'target' as aiming picks this. The blood carries a hormone to all parts of the body; specificity comes from receptors on target cells, not from the route the hormone takes.

mcqs.q: After a meal, glucose absorbed in the small intestine is used for cell respiration in the leg muscles. How does the blood system integrate these two organs?
options: The glucose passes to the muscles directly through the tissues, since blood only carries oxygen.
Nerves running from the intestine to the leg muscles carry the glucose molecules along their fibres.
Each organ makes the glucose that it needs for itself, so no transport between them is needed.
Blood carries the glucose from capillaries in the intestine wall to the muscle cells.
mcqs.specStatementText: Nerves, hormones and blood link organs together
mcqs.explain: The blood system integrates organs by transporting materials between them: glucose absorbed by the villi enters the blood and is carried, via the liver and the general circulation, to muscle cells that respire it.
rationales: A student who links blood only with oxygen picks this. Glucose cannot diffuse the length of the body through tissues; it is absorbed into the blood and delivered by the circulation, as are amino acids, urea and hormones.
A student who thinks nerves are the body's general delivery system picks this. Nerves conduct electrical impulses; they do not transport materials. Glucose is carried in the blood plasma.

A student who sees organs as self-sufficient picks this. Muscles do not make glucose; they depend on glucose absorbed by the intestine or released by the liver and delivered by the blood, which is exactly why the organs must be integrated.

The blood system integrates organs by transporting materials between them: glucose absorbed by the villi enters the blood and is carried, via the liver and the general circulation, to muscle cells that respire it.

mcqs.q: A tennis player watches the ball, hears it hit the opponent's racket, senses the position of her own arm and remembers where the opponent usually aims. What is the role of her brain in producing her return shot?
options: It combines the information from all these inputs with stored memory and uses the result to decide the response.
It processes each input in its own region, and each region sends its own response to the muscles.
It only supplies timing, because the movement itself is stored in the arm muscles from previous practice.
It uses only the input she is consciously aware of, sight, since the brain cannot process input unconsciously.
mcqs.specStatementText: The brain combines inputs, learns and remembers
mcqs.explain: The brain is the central information integration organ: it processes information combined from several inputs (sight, hearing, body position) together with learning and memory, and produces one coordinated response.
rationales: The brain is the central information integration organ: it processes information combined from several inputs (sight, hearing, body position) together with learning and memory, and produces one coordinated response.

A student who pictures the brain as a set of independent sensory modules picks this. Separate responses from each sense would conflict; the brain integrates the inputs before a single motor output is sent.
A student who takes 'muscle memory' literally picks this. Learning and memory are functions of the brain; muscles store nothing and contract only when motor neurons stimulate them.
A student who thinks all brain processing is conscious picks this. Much of the brain's integration, such as using the sense of arm position, happens without awareness; all the inputs contribute.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the spinal cord and unconscious processes is correct?
options: The spinal cord only conducts impulses between the body and the brain, so every kind of integration must take place in the brain itself.
The spinal cord integrates some unconscious responses, receiving sensory input and sending motor output without the brain deciding.
Every unconscious process is integrated in the spinal cord, because everything that the brain does is conscious.
Reflexes are called unconscious only because the brain makes the decision too quickly for us to be aware of doing so.
mcqs.specStatementText: The spinal cord integrates responses we are not aware of
mcqs.explain: The spinal cord is an integrating centre for unconscious processes such as reflexes: its grey matter contains interneurons and synapses that link sensory input to motor output without the cerebral hemispheres deciding.
rationales: A student who pictures the spinal cord as a cable picks this. The cord conducts impulses, but its grey matter also integrates reflexes; a withdrawal reflex is completed before the brain is involved.

The spinal cord is an integrating centre for unconscious processes such as reflexes: its grey matter contains interneurons and synapses that link sensory input to motor output without the cerebral hemispheres deciding.
A student who equates 'brain' with 'conscious' picks this. Many unconscious processes, such as control of heart rate and ventilation, are integrated in the medulla, which is part of the brain.

A student who cannot imagine a response without the brain deciding picks this. A spinal reflex does not involve a decision by the brain at all; the response is produced in the spinal cord and the brain learns of it afterwards.

mcqs.q: What is the function of sensory neurons?
options: They carry impulses out from the central nervous system to the receptors that must then respond.
They detect every stimulus themselves, so the body needs no separate receptor cells.
They convey impulses from receptor cells to the spinal cord and the cerebral hemispheres.
They are the nerves that connect each sense organ to the brain, each made of one long fibre.
mcqs.specStatementText: Sensory neurons carry messages in
mcqs.explain: Sensory neurons convey messages from receptor cells to the central nervous system, providing the input to the spinal cord and cerebral hemispheres.
rationales: A student who has swapped the two neuron types picks this. Impulses out of the CNS travel along motor neurons to effectors; receptors do not respond, they detect. Sensory neurons carry input inwards only.

A student who generalizes from the free nerve ending of the pain reflex picks this. In most sense organs, separate receptor cells (such as photoreceptors in the retina) detect the stimulus and signal to the sensory neuron.
Sensory neurons convey messages from receptor cells to the central nervous system, providing the input to the spinal cord and cerebral hemispheres.

A student who treats nerve and neuron as the same thing picks this. A sensory neuron is a single cell; a nerve is a bundle of fibres from many neurons, usually including both sensory and motor fibres.

mcqs.q: A person decides to straighten their arm. How does output from the cerebral hemispheres produce this movement?
options: Motor neurons stimulate the triceps to contract and other motor neurons stimulate the biceps to lengthen actively.
Sensory neurons carry the command from the cerebral hemispheres down to the triceps, causing it to contract.
Epinephrine released into the blood stimulates the triceps to contract, because hormones control the skeletal muscles.
Motor neurons stimulate the triceps to contract, and the biceps relaxes because it is no longer stimulated.
mcqs.specStatementText: Motor neurons carry commands out to muscles
mcqs.explain: Output from the cerebral hemispheres reaches muscles through motor neurons, which stimulate contraction. The triceps contracts to straighten the arm; the biceps relaxes because stimulation of it is withdrawn, and it is lengthened passively.
rationales: A student who thinks a nerve can drive a muscle in both directions picks this. Muscles can only be stimulated to contract; the biceps is lengthened by the contraction of its antagonist, not by a signal to extend.
A student who has swapped the neuron types picks this. Sensory neurons carry input to the CNS; output from the cerebral hemispheres to muscles is through motor neurons.

A student who thinks epinephrine causes muscle action picks this. Skeletal muscle contracts when stimulated by motor neurons; epinephrine prepares the body for activity but does not command a movement.

Output from the cerebral hemispheres reaches muscles through motor neurons, which stimulate contraction. The triceps contracts to straighten the arm; the biceps relaxes because stimulation of it is withdrawn, and it is lengthened passively.

mcqs.q: A transverse section of a nerve shows an outer layer of connective tissue enclosing many small circular profiles. Some profiles have a thick pale ring around a central dot; others have no ring. What does the section show?
options: A bundle of nerve fibres inside a protective sheath, the ringed profiles being myelinated fibres and the rest unmyelinated.
Several separate nerves, because the thick pale ring around each ringed profile is a nerve's protective sheath.
A bundle of fibres in which the profiles without a ring are damaged fibres that have lost their myelin.
A single neuron cut across, with the outer layer being its cell membrane and the profiles its organelles.
mcqs.specStatementText: A nerve is a bundle of many fibres
mcqs.explain: A nerve is a bundle of nerve fibres enclosed in a protective sheath. In transverse section each myelinated fibre shows its axon (the dot) surrounded by the pale, fatty myelin sheath; unmyelinated fibres are bare axons.
rationales: A nerve is a bundle of nerve fibres enclosed in a protective sheath. In transverse section each myelinated fibre shows its axon (the dot) surrounded by the pale, fatty myelin sheath; unmyelinated fibres are bare axons.

A student who confuses the myelin sheath with the nerve's protective sheath picks this. The ring around a single axon is myelin; the protective sheath is the connective tissue layer around the whole bundle.
A student who believes every healthy fibre is myelinated picks this. Normal nerves contain both myelinated and unmyelinated fibres; the unmyelinated ones simply conduct more slowly.
A student who treats a nerve as one cell picks this. Each circular profile is the fibre of a different neuron; the outer layer is connective tissue enclosing hundreds or thousands of such fibres.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the relationship between a nerve and a neuron is correct?
options: A nerve and a neuron are the same structure; nerve is simply the word used for a neuron long enough to be seen unaided.
A nerve is a bundle of nerve fibres from many neurons and usually contains fibres of both sensory and motor neurons.
A nerve contains the fibres of many neurons, but all the fibres in any one nerve are either sensory or motor.
A nerve is a group of neurons wrapped together in a single myelin sheath, which acts as its protective sheath.
mcqs.specStatementText: A nerve is a bundle of many fibres
mcqs.explain: Nerves are bundles of nerve fibres of both sensory and motor neurons, enclosed in a protective sheath. A neuron is a single cell whose fibre is one of many in the bundle.
rationales: A student who uses the two words interchangeably picks this. A neuron is one cell; a nerve is a visible bundle of the fibres of many neurons, which is why it can be seen without a microscope.
Nerves are bundles of nerve fibres of both sensory and motor neurons, enclosed in a protective sheath. A neuron is a single cell whose fibre is one of many in the bundle.
A student who extends the reflex-arc labels to whole nerves picks this. Most nerves are mixed, carrying impulses towards the CNS in sensory fibres and away from it in motor fibres.

A student who merges the two kinds of sheath picks this. Myelin surrounds individual fibres; the protective sheath of the nerve is connective tissue around the whole bundle, and some fibres in it have no myelin.

mcqs.q: A person touches a hot pan and withdraws their hand before feeling any pain. Which sequence describes the reflex arc that produced the withdrawal?
options: free nerve ending → sensory neuron → spinal cord → cerebral hemispheres → motor neuron → skeletal muscle of the arm
free nerve ending → sensory neuron → interneuron in the spinal cord grey matter → motor neuron → smooth muscle of the arm
free nerve ending → sensory neuron → interneuron in spinal cord grey matter → motor neuron → skeletal muscle of the arm
skeletal muscle of the arm → sensory neuron → interneuron in the grey matter of the spinal cord → motor neuron → free nerve ending
mcqs.specStatementText: The pain reflex withdraws the hand before you feel it
mcqs.explain: The pain reflex arc has a free sensory nerve ending as the receptor, a sensory neuron into the spinal cord, a single interneuron in the grey matter, a motor neuron out, and skeletal muscle as the effector.
rationales: A student who thinks the brain must decide picks this. The reflex is integrated in the spinal cord; impulses do also travel to the brain, but the withdrawal has already been triggered before they arrive.
A student who thinks involuntary responses must use involuntary muscle picks this. The effector in the pain reflex is skeletal muscle; the arm has no smooth muscle that could move it.

The pain reflex arc has a free sensory nerve ending as the receptor, a sensory neuron into the spinal cord, a single interneuron in the grey matter, a motor neuron out, and skeletal muscle as the effector.
A student who has swapped receptor and effector picks this. The free nerve ending detects the stimulus and so comes first; the muscle carries out the response and so comes last.

mcqs.q: In the pain withdrawal reflex, the hand is pulled away before the person becomes aware of any pain. Which explanation accounts for this order of events?
options: The brain feels the pain first and decides to withdraw the hand, but this decision is made too fast to be noticed.
The spinal cord only conducts impulses, so the brain must have ordered the withdrawal and awareness of pain simply lags behind.
The arm muscle acts as the receptor as well as the effector, so it responds before the hand has sent any impulses at all.
The reflex is completed in the spinal cord, and impulses giving awareness of pain reach the brain only later.
mcqs.specStatementText: The pain reflex withdraws the hand before you feel it
mcqs.explain: The reflex arc passes through a single interneuron in the spinal cord, so the motor output leaves before impulses have travelled up the cord to the cerebral hemispheres, where the pain is perceived.
rationales: A student who puts feeling before action picks this. If the brain decided, awareness of pain would come before or with the movement, not after it; the observed order shows the brain was not in the loop.
A student who thinks the spinal cord cannot process anything picks this. The cord's grey matter integrates the reflex itself; that is why the movement can precede the brain's involvement.

A student who confuses receptor with effector picks this. The receptor is the free nerve ending in the hand; the muscle responds only when a motor neuron stimulates it, after the impulse has passed through the spinal cord.
The reflex arc passes through a single interneuron in the spinal cord, so the motor output leaves before impulses have travelled up the cord to the cerebral hemispheres, where the pain is perceived.

mcqs.q: Which statement describes the role of the cerebellum in the control of body movements?
options: It coordinates the contraction of skeletal muscles so that movements are smooth and accurate, and it maintains balance.
It initiates voluntary movements by deciding which skeletal muscles should contract and at what moment.
It has no role in balance, which is maintained entirely by the semicircular canals within the inner ear.
It controls involuntary movements such as the heartbeat and breathing rather than any of the skeletal muscles.
mcqs.specStatementText: The cerebellum makes movement smooth and keeps balance
mcqs.explain: The cerebellum coordinates skeletal muscle contraction and balance, using sensory information to adjust the timing and strength of contractions commanded by the cerebral hemispheres.
rationales: The cerebellum coordinates skeletal muscle contraction and balance, using sensory information to adjust the timing and strength of contractions commanded by the cerebral hemispheres.
A student who reads 'controls movement' as 'commands movement' picks this. Voluntary movements are initiated by the cerebral hemispheres; the cerebellum coordinates them.

A student who takes 'organ of balance' literally picks this. The inner ear detects movement of the head; the cerebellum integrates this with other input and adjusts muscle contraction to keep the body balanced.
A student who confuses the cerebellum with the medulla picks this. Heart rate and ventilation are coordinated by the medulla; the cerebellum's role is with skeletal muscle.

mcqs.q: Blood melatonin concentration in a person was measured over 24 hours. It was low from 08:00 to 20:00, rose from 21:00, was highest between 02:00 and 04:00 and had fallen by 07:00. Which statement explains this pattern and its effect?
options: Falling asleep stimulates the pineal gland to secrete melatonin, which is why the level rises after bedtime.
The pineal gland secretes melatonin while the eyes detect little light, and high melatonin at night promotes sleep.
The pituitary gland secretes melatonin in response to darkness, and its high level makes the person sleepy.
Light stimulates melatonin secretion during the day; the night-time peak is melatonin that has not yet been broken down.
mcqs.specStatementText: Melatonin from the pineal gland sets the sleep cycle
mcqs.explain: Melatonin is secreted by the pineal gland in a diurnal pattern: darkness allows secretion and light suppresses it. The night-time peak promotes sleep, helping to establish the cycle of sleeping and waking.
rationales: A student who reverses cause and effect picks this. Secretion begins to rise from 21:00, in the dark, before sleep; the rise promotes sleep rather than being caused by it.

Melatonin is secreted by the pineal gland in a diurnal pattern: darkness allows secretion and light suppresses it. The night-time peak promotes sleep, helping to establish the cycle of sleeping and waking.
A student who attributes every brain hormone to the master gland picks this. Melatonin is secreted by the pineal gland, not the pituitary; the rest of the description is correct.
A student who expects light to be the stimulus picks this. Light suppresses secretion, which is why the level is low all day; the night-time peak is newly secreted melatonin, not a leftover.

mcqs.q: A student who uses a bright screen until midnight finds it hard to fall asleep and wakes late the next morning. Using the role of melatonin in circadian rhythms, which explanation is best supported?
options: Light from the screen stimulates melatonin secretion, and the high melatonin level keeps the student awake until it has all been used up.
No melatonin was secreted because the student stayed awake, since the pineal gland only begins to secrete it once sleep has begun.
Light from the screen suppresses evening melatonin secretion, delaying the rise that promotes sleep and shifting the cycle later.
Melatonin is secreted by the pituitary gland, not in response to light, so the screen could not have altered its timing.
mcqs.specStatementText: Melatonin from the pineal gland sets the sleep cycle
mcqs.explain: Light detected by the eyes suppresses secretion by the pineal gland. Evening light delays the normal rise of melatonin, so sleepiness comes later and the whole sleep–wake cycle, including waking, is shifted later.
rationales: A student who thinks light stimulates melatonin picks this. Melatonin promotes sleep, not wakefulness, and light suppresses it; the student stays awake because melatonin is low, not high.
A student who thinks sleep causes melatonin picks this. Secretion normally rises in the evening before sleep; what delayed it here was the light, not the wakefulness.

Light detected by the eyes suppresses secretion by the pineal gland. Evening light delays the normal rise of melatonin, so sleepiness comes later and the whole sleep–wake cycle, including waking, is shifted later.

A student who attributes melatonin to the pituitary picks this. Melatonin is secreted by the pineal gland, and its secretion is suppressed by light detected by the eyes, which is exactly why evening screen light delays sleep (C3.1.11).

mcqs.q: A sprinter waits for the starting signal and epinephrine is secreted into the blood. Which set of effects of epinephrine helps to facilitate intense contraction of the leg muscles during the race?
options: Faster heart rate and an equal increase in blood flow to every organ, including the gut, the skin and the kidneys.
Direct transfer of energy from the adrenal glands to the leg muscle fibres, so that they can contract more strongly.
Direct stimulation of the leg muscle fibres to contract, taking over from the motor neurons for the duration of the race.
Faster heart rate, wider bronchioles, glycogen breakdown in the liver and more blood flow to skeletal muscle.
mcqs.specStatementText: Epinephrine readies the body for hard exercise
mcqs.explain: These widespread effects of epinephrine increase the delivery of oxygen and glucose to the muscles: more cardiac output, easier ventilation, higher blood glucose and blood diverted to skeletal muscle, allowing intense cell respiration and contraction.
rationales: A student who reasons that more output means more blood everywhere picks this. Epinephrine redistributes blood: vessels to the gut and skin constrict while those to skeletal muscle dilate.
A student who takes 'adrenaline rush' as a burst of energy picks this. Epinephrine is a signal; the energy for contraction comes from cell respiration of glucose in the muscle.
A student who thinks the hormone commands the movement picks this. Skeletal muscle contracts only when stimulated by motor neurons; epinephrine prepares the body but does not replace nervous control.

These widespread effects of epinephrine increase the delivery of oxygen and glucose to the muscles: more cardiac output, easier ventilation, higher blood glucose and blood diverted to skeletal muscle, allowing intense cell respiration and contraction.

mcqs.q: Which statement describes how the hypothalamus and the pituitary gland control the endocrine system?
options: The hypothalamus controls the pituitary gland, which secretes hormones that act on body tissues or that control other endocrine glands.
The pituitary gland controls the other endocrine glands by itself; the hypothalamus is part of the nervous system and plays no role.
The hypothalamus controls the pituitary gland by nerve impulses only, because the hypothalamus cannot secrete any hormones.
Each endocrine gland monitors the blood and secretes its hormone independently, so no gland controls any other gland.
mcqs.specStatementText: The hypothalamus runs the pituitary, which runs other glands
mcqs.explain: The hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems and controls the pituitary. Pituitary hormones act on tissues directly or regulate other glands, so the two structures together control much of the endocrine system.
rationales: The hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems and controls the pituitary. Pituitary hormones act on tissues directly or regulate other glands, so the two structures together control much of the endocrine system.
A student who stops at 'master gland' picks this. The pituitary is itself controlled by the hypothalamus, which is the link between nervous input and hormonal output.
A student who thinks a brain region cannot be endocrine picks this. The hypothalamus does produce hormones, and some of these control the pituitary's secretion.

A student who generalizes from the pancreas picks this. Several pituitary hormones control the secretion of other glands, such as the thyroid gland and the gonads, so the endocrine system is hierarchically controlled.

mcqs.q: Which statement gives the location and the function of the receptors that provide sensory input for the control of heart rate?
options: Baroreceptors and chemoreceptors are both in the wall of the heart, where they monitor the pressure and the chemistry of the blood as it passes through it.
Baroreceptors in the aorta and carotid arteries monitor blood pressure; chemoreceptors there and in the medulla monitor pH, oxygen and carbon dioxide.
Baroreceptors in the aorta monitor blood pressure and chemoreceptors in the carotid arteries monitor only the concentration of oxygen.
Baroreceptors and chemoreceptors are both located in the medulla, which monitors the pressure and chemistry of the blood flowing through it.
mcqs.specStatementText: Heart rate is adjusted by feedback from pressure and chemical sensors
mcqs.explain: Baroreceptors are stretch receptors in the walls of the aorta and carotid arteries. Chemoreceptors in the same arteries and in the medulla monitor blood pH and the concentrations of oxygen and carbon dioxide. Both send impulses to the medulla.
rationales: A student who expects the heart to monitor itself picks this. The receptors are in the major arteries leaving the heart and in the medulla, not in the heart wall.

Baroreceptors are stretch receptors in the walls of the aorta and carotid arteries. Chemoreceptors in the same arteries and in the medulla monitor blood pH and the concentrations of oxygen and carbon dioxide. Both send impulses to the medulla.

A student who thinks oxygen is the only chemical sensed picks this. Chemoreceptors monitor pH and carbon dioxide as well as oxygen, and they are found in the aorta and medulla as well as the carotid arteries.
A student who places all the sensors in the brain picks this. The medulla does contain chemoreceptors, but baroreceptors are in the artery walls, where stretch can be detected directly.

mcqs.q: A person stands up quickly and their blood pressure falls for a few seconds. Which sequence describes the feedback response that restores blood pressure?
options: Baroreceptors detect the fall and the medulla sends impulses along the vagus nerve to reduce heart rate, because a lower rate lets the pressure recover.
The medulla sends the impulses that cause each heartbeat more frequently, because the heart cannot beat at all unless the medulla drives it.
Baroreceptors in the arteries send fewer impulses to the medulla, which sends sympathetic impulses that raise heart rate and stroke volume.
Baroreceptors in the heart wall detect the fall in pressure and the heart raises its own rate without any involvement of the medulla.
mcqs.specStatementText: Heart rate is adjusted by feedback from pressure and chemical sensors
mcqs.explain: Lower pressure stretches the artery walls less, so baroreceptor impulses to the medulla decrease. The medulla responds by increasing sympathetic impulses to the heart, raising heart rate and stroke volume so that pressure rises: negative feedback.
rationales: A student who has the direction of the feedback reversed picks this. Reducing heart rate would lower pressure further; the vagus nerve slows the heart when pressure is too high, not too low.
A student who thinks the medulla generates the heartbeat picks this. The heart beats on its own; the medulla's nerve impulses only speed it up or slow it down and change its stroke volume.

Lower pressure stretches the artery walls less, so baroreceptor impulses to the medulla decrease. The medulla responds by increasing sympathetic impulses to the heart, raising heart rate and stroke volume so that pressure rises: negative feedback.
A student who locates the receptors in the heart picks this. Baroreceptors are in the aorta and carotid arteries, and the response is coordinated by the medulla, not by the heart itself.

mcqs.q: During a run, a student's blood carbon dioxide concentration rises, blood pH falls from 7.40 to 7.32 and ventilation rate rises from 12 to 30 breaths per minute. Which statement correctly links these changes?
options: The extra carbon dioxide makes the blood more alkaline, as shown by the fall in pH, and chemoreceptors in the brainstem respond to this by increasing ventilation.
Carbon dioxide is a gas and so cannot change pH; the fall in pH is due to lactic acid from the muscles, which is detected by chemoreceptors in the lungs.
The student consciously decides to breathe faster on feeling out of breath, and the changes in carbon dioxide and pH are consequences of this, not causes.
Carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid, lowering pH; brainstem chemoreceptors detect this and the medulla increases signals to the breathing muscles.
mcqs.specStatementText: Ventilation rate is adjusted by feedback from blood pH
mcqs.explain: Carbon dioxide from increased cell respiration dissolves to form carbonic acid, which lowers blood pH. Chemoreceptors in the brainstem detect the change and the medulla increases signals to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles, raising ventilation rate and removing carbon dioxide.
rationales: A student who confuses the direction of the pH scale picks this. A fall in pH means the blood has become more acidic, which is what carbonic acid formed from carbon dioxide causes.

A student who thinks only lactic acid acidifies blood picks this. Dissolved carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid and is the usual cause of the fall in pH, and the chemoreceptors involved are in the brainstem, not the lungs.

A student who thinks breathing is voluntary picks this. Ventilation rate is raised automatically by the medulla in response to chemoreceptor input; the rise in carbon dioxide and fall in pH are the causes of faster breathing, not its results.

Carbon dioxide from increased cell respiration dissolves to form carbonic acid, which lowers blood pH. Chemoreceptors in the brainstem detect the change and the medulla increases signals to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles, raising ventilation rate and removing carbon dioxide.

mcqs.q: A person swallows a mouthful of food. Which statement correctly describes how the movement of this food through the digestive system is controlled?
options: Starting the swallow is voluntary and controlled by the CNS; peristalsis along the oesophagus and gut is involuntary and controlled by the ENS.
The CNS controls the whole process, sending an impulse to the gut muscles for each wave of peristalsis until faeces are egested.
After swallowing, the food moves down the oesophagus and the intestine mainly under gravity, with muscle contraction only assisting.
Swallowing is a reflex from the moment food enters the mouth, so no stage of the movement is under voluntary control.
mcqs.specStatementText: Swallowing and egestion are voluntary; peristalsis in between is not
mcqs.explain: Initiation of swallowing (and egestion of faeces) is under voluntary control by the CNS. Between these points, peristalsis is under involuntary control by the enteric nervous system, which coordinates the passage of material through the gut.
rationales: Initiation of swallowing (and egestion of faeces) is under voluntary control by the CNS. Between these points, peristalsis is under involuntary control by the enteric nervous system, which coordinates the passage of material through the gut.
A student who assumes every muscle is driven by the CNS picks this. The gut wall has its own enteric nervous system, which controls peristalsis without instructions from the brain or spinal cord.
A student who thinks food falls through the gut picks this. Peristalsis, coordinated by the ENS, moves material along the gut regardless of orientation; gravity is not required.
A student who has heard swallowing called a reflex picks this. The initiation of swallowing is a voluntary act controlled by the CNS; only the peristalsis that follows is involuntary.

mcqs.q: Two students each measured the angle of curvature of the same seedling shoot five times with a protractor. Student A recorded 28°, 29°, 28°, 29°, 28°. Student B recorded 22°, 35°, 30°, 26°, 37°. A later check showed that the true angle was 35° and that Student A had aligned the protractor with the edge of the pot instead of the vertical part of the stem. Which conclusion is justified?
options: Student A's measurements are both precise and accurate, because five repeats that agree so closely must lie close to the true value.
Student A's measurements are precise but not accurate, because a systematic error shifted all of them away from the true value.
Student A could have obtained an accurate mean by taking more repeats, because repetition removes systematic error.
Student B's readings are qualitative rather than quantitative, because they vary too much between repeats to be measurements.
mcqs.specStatementText: Recording tropisms: diagrams and angles
mcqs.explain: A's repeats agree within 1°, so they are precise, but all are 6–7° below the true value because of a systematic error in aligning the protractor. Precision (agreement between repeats) does not guarantee accuracy (closeness to the true value).
rationales: A student who treats precise and accurate as synonyms picks this. The repeats agree with each other but not with the true value of 35°; consistent measurements can all share the same systematic error.

A's repeats agree within 1°, so they are precise, but all are 6–7° below the true value because of a systematic error in aligning the protractor. Precision (agreement between repeats) does not guarantee accuracy (closeness to the true value).
A student who thinks repeats cure all error picks this. More repeats would reduce random scatter but every repeat would carry the same alignment error, so the mean would stay near 28°.
A student who judges the quantitative/qualitative distinction by data quality picks this. B's readings are numerical measurements in degrees, so they are quantitative; they are simply imprecise.

mcqs.q: Students investigating phototropism recorded three observations of seedlings lit from one side: (1) a labelled drawing showing the shoot curved towards the lamp; (2) 'the shoots bent much more than those of the control'; (3) an angle of curvature of 32° measured with a protractor. Which classification is correct?
options: (2) and (3) are quantitative because both describe the amount of bending; (1) is qualitative.
Only (3) is an observation; (1) and (2) are not data as they have no number.
(1) and (2) are qualitative observations and (3) is a quantitative observation.
(1) is quantitative because a careful scale drawing records the exact shape of the shoot.
mcqs.specStatementText: Recording tropisms: diagrams and angles
mcqs.explain: A drawing and a comparative description record features without numerical measurement, so they are qualitative. A measured angle in degrees is a quantitative observation.
rationales: A student who thinks any statement about 'how much' is quantitative picks this. 'Much more' is a comparison in words with no measured value, so (2) is qualitative.
A student who thinks only numbers count as data picks this. Diagrams recording the direction of curvature are qualitative data that the IB expects students to gather; they are valid observations.
A drawing and a comparative description record features without numerical measurement, so they are qualitative. A measured angle in degrees is a quantitative observation.
A student who equates careful with quantitative picks this. However carefully made, a drawing is a description of shape, not a numerical measurement, so it is a qualitative observation.

mcqs.q: A seedling is grown in a box with a window on its left side only. After two days the shoot has curved towards the window. Which statement explains the curvature?
options: Cells on the lit left side elongated more because the light supplied the energy for their growth, pulling the shoot over.
The existing tissues of the shoot bent towards the window in the way an animal turns its head, without any growth occurring.
Light destroyed all the auxin on the left side, so cells there stopped growing while the cells on the right grew normally.
Cells on the shaded right side elongated more than cells on the lit left side, so growth bent the shoot to the left.
mcqs.specStatementText: Shoots grow towards light from the side
mcqs.explain: Positive phototropism is a directional growth response: auxin accumulates on the shaded side, cells there elongate more, and the unequal growth bends the shoot towards the light.
rationales: A student who reasons that growth happens where the light is picks this. If the lit side grew more the shoot would bend away from the light; it is the shaded side that elongates faster.
A student who thinks of tropism as movement picks this. A tropism is a growth response; the curvature is produced by new elongation of cells over hours to days, not by movement of existing tissue.
A student who believes light breaks down auxin picks this. Auxin is redistributed by efflux carriers towards the shaded side, not destroyed; the lit side still grows, just more slowly.
Positive phototropism is a directional growth response: auxin accumulates on the shaded side, cells there elongate more, and the unequal growth bends the shoot towards the light.

mcqs.q: Which statement about phytohormones is correct?
options: Plants use a variety of chemicals, including auxins, cytokinins and ethylene, as signals controlling growth, development and responses to stimuli.
Auxin is the only phytohormone, and all plant growth, development and responses to stimuli are controlled by its concentration.
Phytohormones are secreted by glands in the plant and carried in the xylem to all parts, just as animal hormones are carried in blood.
Phytohormones diffuse freely into and out of cells, so their concentration ends up the same in every part of the plant.
mcqs.specStatementText: Plants signal with a variety of chemicals
mcqs.explain: Phytohormones are signalling chemicals controlling growth, development and response to stimuli in plants, and a variety of different chemicals serve this role.
rationales: Phytohormones are signalling chemicals controlling growth, development and response to stimuli in plants, and a variety of different chemicals serve this role.

A student for whom auxin stands for all plant signalling picks this. Cytokinins, ethylene and other chemicals are phytohormones with their own roles, such as cytokinin in shoot growth and ethylene in ripening.
A student who transfers the animal model to plants picks this. Plants have no glands; phytohormones are made in tissues such as shoot and root tips and move from cell to cell or in vascular tissue.
A student who assumes diffusion is symmetrical picks this. Auxin, for example, enters cells freely but leaves only through efflux carriers, which allows concentration gradients to be set up.

mcqs.q: In a column of cells in a shoot, every cell has its auxin efflux carriers concentrated in the membrane at its lower (basal) end. What happens to auxin in this tissue?
options: Auxin diffuses in and out of every cell across all parts of its membrane, so the carriers make no difference and the auxin stays evenly spread throughout.
Auxin enters each cell freely by diffusion but can leave only through the basal carriers, so it is transported downwards and accumulates below.
The efflux carriers pump auxin into each cell from the cell below, so auxin is transported upwards and accumulates at the shoot tip.
Auxin is carried in the xylem sap, so the position of the carriers in the cell membranes has no effect on where it accumulates.
mcqs.specStatementText: Efflux carriers push auxin one way through a tissue
mcqs.explain: Auxin diffuses freely into cells but not out. With every cell's efflux carriers on its lower side, auxin is pumped out of the base of each cell into the next cell down, so it moves in one direction through the tissue and becomes concentrated lower in the plant.
rationales: A student who thinks auxin leaves cells as freely as it enters picks this. Auxin cannot diffuse out of cells; it exits only through the efflux carriers, whose position therefore sets the direction of transport.

Auxin diffuses freely into cells but not out. With every cell's efflux carriers on its lower side, auxin is pumped out of the base of each cell into the next cell down, so it moves in one direction through the tissue and becomes concentrated lower in the plant.
A student who reads efflux as influx picks this. Efflux carriers pump auxin out of the cell; carriers on the basal side therefore move auxin downwards, away from the shoot tip.

A student who expects a bloodstream-like transport system picks this. Directional auxin transport through tissues is from cell to cell via efflux carriers, and their position determines where auxin becomes concentrated.

mcqs.q: Which statement describes how auxin promotes the elongation of a plant cell?
options: It stimulates the cell to divide by mitosis, so the tissue becomes longer because it contains a larger number of cells.
It stimulates secretion of hydrogen ions into the cell wall, where the acid dissolves the cellulose molecules so the wall can be rebuilt longer.
It promotes hydrogen ion secretion into the apoplast; the acidified wall has its cellulose cross links loosened and can stretch.
It acidifies the cytoplasm, and the increased acidity inside the cell draws in water by osmosis so that the cell swells and lengthens.
mcqs.specStatementText: Auxin loosens cell walls so cells elongate
mcqs.explain: Auxin promotes hydrogen ion secretion into the apoplast. The acidified cell wall has its cross links between cellulose molecules loosened, which facilitates elongation as the cell takes up water.
rationales: A student who equates growth with division picks this. Auxin's promotion of growth in this context is by cell elongation, not by increasing cell number.

A student who hears 'acidify' as 'dissolve' picks this. The low pH loosens the cross links between cellulose molecules; the cellulose itself is not broken down, and the wall stretches rather than being rebuilt.
Auxin promotes hydrogen ion secretion into the apoplast. The acidified cell wall has its cross links between cellulose molecules loosened, which facilitates elongation as the cell takes up water.

A student who places the acid inside the cell picks this. Hydrogen ions are secreted out of the cytoplasm into the apoplast; it is the wall that is acidified and loosened, allowing the cell to elongate.

mcqs.q: A plant's roots are damaged, reducing the number of root tips. Using the interaction between auxin and cytokinin, what is the predicted effect on the shoots?
options: Less auxin is transported to the shoots, because root tips are where auxin is produced, so shoot growth is reduced.
Shoot growth is unaffected, because cytokinin acts only in the roots where it is made, and auxin only in the shoots.
Shoot growth is unaffected, because auxin, the only phytohormone, is made in the undamaged shoot tips.
Less cytokinin reaches the shoots, so shoot growth is reduced to match the smaller root system.
mcqs.specStatementText: Root and shoot tips signal to each other
mcqs.explain: Root tips produce cytokinin, which is transported to the shoots and promotes their growth. Fewer root tips means less cytokinin reaching the shoots, so shoot growth is restrained: this is how the interaction keeps root and shoot growth integrated.
rationales: A student who has swapped the sources picks this. Auxin is produced in shoot tips and transported to the roots; it is cytokinin that root tips produce and send to the shoots.
A student who expects each hormone to act locally picks this. Each hormone is transported to the other organ, which is precisely what allows root damage to influence shoot growth.
A student who thinks auxin is the sole plant hormone picks this. Cytokinin from the root tips is also needed for shoot growth, so damage to the roots does affect the shoots.

Root tips produce cytokinin, which is transported to the shoots and promotes their growth. Fewer root tips means less cytokinin reaching the shoots, so shoot growth is restrained: this is how the interaction keeps root and shoot growth integrated.

mcqs.q: The concentration of ethylene in the air around a ripening fruit was measured each day: 0.1, 0.3, 1.2 and 4.8 ppm on days 1 to 4, by which time the fruit was fully ripe. Which statement best interprets these data?
options: Ethylene stimulates ripening and ripening stimulates more ethylene production, so the concentration rises faster and faster: positive feedback.
Ethylene production is under negative feedback, so each rise in ethylene reduces further production and ripening proceeds steadily.
The mechanism is positive feedback because ripening benefits the plant; a harmful process with this pattern would be negative feedback.
Ethylene acts only inside the fruit that produces it, so the rising concentration in the air is a waste product with no effect on ripening.
mcqs.specStatementText: Ethylene and ripening drive each other
mcqs.explain: The concentration rises by a larger amount each day (0.2, 0.9, 3.6 ppm), an accelerating rise characteristic of positive feedback: ethylene stimulates the changes of ripening, and ripening stimulates increased ethylene production.
rationales: The concentration rises by a larger amount each day (0.2, 0.9, 3.6 ppm), an accelerating rise characteristic of positive feedback: ethylene stimulates the changes of ripening, and ripening stimulates increased ethylene production.
A student who assumes all feedback is negative picks this. Negative feedback would hold the concentration steady; the data show an accelerating rise, which only positive feedback produces.

A student who reads 'positive' as 'good' picks this. Positive feedback describes a response that increases the stimulus, whatever its value to the organism; the accelerating rise is what makes this positive feedback.

A student who thinks a hormone must stay inside the organism picks this. Ethylene is a gas that diffuses through the air and stimulates ripening in neighbouring fruits; it is a signal, not a waste product.

mcqs.q: Why is positive feedback in ethylene production beneficial to a plant?
options: Positive feedback is, by definition, feedback that benefits the organism, so its benefit to the plant needs no further explanation.
It makes ripening rapid and synchronized, so the fruits on the plant become attractive to seed-dispersing animals together.
It keeps the rate of ripening slow and steady, so the plant is not left with more ripe fruit than can be dispersed.
It confines ethylene to the fruit that makes it, so one over-ripe fruit cannot make the others on the plant ripen.
mcqs.specStatementText: Ethylene and ripening drive each other
mcqs.explain: Positive feedback ensures that once ripening starts it accelerates and, because ethylene spreads between fruits, all ripen together; a synchronized crop of ripe fruit attracts the animals that disperse the seeds.
rationales: A student who gives 'positive' its everyday meaning picks this. The term describes a response that amplifies the stimulus; whether it is beneficial has to be explained by its effects, here rapid, synchronized ripening.

Positive feedback ensures that once ripening starts it accelerates and, because ethylene spreads between fruits, all ripen together; a synchronized crop of ripe fruit attracts the animals that disperse the seeds.
A student who thinks feedback always stabilizes picks this. Positive feedback accelerates ripening rather than steadying it; the benefit is that ripening is rapid and synchronized.
A student who thinks ethylene stays within its fruit picks this. Ethylene is a gas that diffuses between fruits, and this spread is part of what synchronizes ripening across the plant.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025); topic C3.1 Integration of body systems

specStatements.text: Parts of a living system must work together
Cells build tissues, organs and systems, and new properties emerge
Nerves, hormones and blood link organs together
The brain combines inputs, learns and remembers
The spinal cord integrates responses we are not aware of
Sensory neurons carry messages in
Motor neurons carry commands out to muscles
A nerve is a bundle of many fibres
The pain reflex withdraws the hand before you feel it
The cerebellum makes movement smooth and keeps balance
Melatonin from the pineal gland sets the sleep cycle
Epinephrine readies the body for hard exercise
The hypothalamus runs the pituitary, which runs other glands
Heart rate is adjusted by feedback from pressure and chemical sensors
Ventilation rate is adjusted by feedback from blood pH
Swallowing and egestion are voluntary; peristalsis in between is not
Recording tropisms: diagrams and angles
Shoots grow towards light from the side
Plants signal with a variety of chemicals
Efflux carriers push auxin one way through a tissue
Auxin loosens cell walls so cells elongate
Root and shoot tips signal to each other
Ethylene and ripening drive each other

scopeNotes.howHonoured: The brain is treated only as the organ that combines information from several inputs and stores the results of experience as learning and memory. No neurotransmitters (fast- or slow-acting), no synaptic mechanisms of memory and no cerebral regions other than those named in other statements of this topic (cerebellum, medulla, hypothalamus, pineal gland) are named or tested.

The cerebellum is described only as coordinating skeletal muscle contraction so that movements are smooth and accurate, and as maintaining balance. Its internal structure, its cell types and its connections to the motor cortex are not mentioned. Its sensory inputs (eyes, inner ear, muscle and joint receptors) are named in c18 and m23 only as context for 'coordination'; no item requires them.

The pituitary is treated as a single gland controlled by the hypothalamus. No object distinguishes the anterior and posterior lobes, names any releasing hormone, describes the portal blood supply or describes neurosecretory cells. m32 states only that the hypothalamus itself secretes hormones that help control the pituitary, without saying which lobe or by what route. Examples of pituitary hormones appear only in a concept definition to illustrate that some act directly on tissues and some control other glands; no item requires them.

Only the voluntary initiation of swallowing, the voluntary control of egestion and the involuntary ENS control of peristalsis between them are tested. The phases of the swallowing reflex, the anatomy of the ENS (myenteric and submucosal plexuses), gut hormones and the sympathetic and parasympathetic influences on the gut are not included.
Only positive phototropism of shoots is named and tested. Gravitropism, thigmotropism, hydrotropism and the response of roots to light are not mentioned in any concept, misconception or item.

omitted.sequence: no authored ordering; would require inventing a sequence
